introduction: This third Sunday of Advent is Gaudete Sunday, from the Latin word for rejoice, and rose vestments may be worn. Zephaniah calls the daughter of Zion to sing, for the Lord is in her midst and rejoices over her. Paul tells us to rejoice in the Lord always. In the Gospel, the crowds ask John the Baptist, What should we do? Let us rejoice that the Lord is near, and ask what he wants of us.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord is near; let us rejoice and bring our needs to God in prayer.
intentions: For the Church: that she may be a joyful witness to the nearness of the Lord. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are anxious or afraid: that the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may guard their hearts. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the poor and those who have nothing: that those who have more may share with them, as John taught. Let us pray to the Lord.
For workers, officials and all who hold power over others: that they may be honest, just and fair. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may ask the Lord sincerely, What should we do, and do it with joy. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: God of joy, you are in our midst and you rejoice over us. Fill us with your peace, and show us how to prepare for the coming of your Son. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: What should we do?
reflection.body:
Halfway through Advent, the Church pauses to rejoice. The prophet Zephaniah calls out: "Sing, daughter of Zion! Shout, Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart." The reason is simple: "The King of Israel, the LORD, is among you." Then comes one of the most tender lines in Scripture: God himself rejoices over his people. "He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love. He will rejoice over you with singing."

Paul writes from prison, yet he says, "Rejoice in the Lord always!" and says it again. His joy does not depend on circumstances but on the Lord's nearness. And he gives a remedy for anxiety: "In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God." Then "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts."

In the Gospel, people from every walk of life come to John the Baptist and ask the same question: "What then must we do?" His answers are practical. To everyone: "He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none." To tax collectors: "Collect no more than that which is appointed to you." To soldiers: do not extort, do not accuse falsely, be content with your wages. Conversion happens in ordinary life and work.

Then John points beyond himself: "he comes who is mightier than I." Christian joy grows when we stop being the center and make room for Christ.

This week, ask John's question for yourself: What should I do? Perhaps give a coat or a meal to someone in need, be honest where you have cut corners, or make peace. And bring your worries to God in prayer, with thanksgiving.
